Thank you, Chair. At the outset, I wish to express our gratitude to you and to the Secretariat for organizing this first meeting of the Open-Ended Technical Experts Group. We also thank the briefers for their interesting briefings. Chairman, recent progress in the manufacturing, the technology, and the design of small arms and light weapons bring about many practical and operational challenges, and also regulatory challenges for our national efforts. In particular, the increasing use of polymer components and parts, and the use of 3D printing for illicit purposes is bound to complicate marking and stock management and tracing efforts as well as holding registers and upholding the law. Polymer parts can pose difficulties where traditional marking methods are not easily applicable or where they are not sufficiently durable. Furthermore, modular weapons can make identifying certain weapons and tracing certain weapons more difficult when parts can be replaced or assembled differently. On 3D printing, this brings about particular concerns, especially when components or weapons are produced outside of the authorized manufacturing chains, which makes their authorization, control, and tracing more difficult. In this context, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia believes that it's important for discussions within this group to remain practical and technical, focused on research and looking for a common understanding of these issues and implementation issues, and without creating any new regulatory obligations that could go beyond the frameworks agreed on in the Programme of Action and the ITI. My delegation believes that any approach that would deal with these emerging issues must be focused on the following. First of all, states must preserve the primary responsibility when it comes to regulating the transfer, manufacturing, and tracing of weapons on their territory, and this in line with domestic legislation. Secondly, responses to new technological evolutions must be in line with the framework of existing obligations, in particular the Programme of Action and the International Tracing Instrument. All responses and measures— none of them should replace these programmes or instruments. Thirdly, international cooperation and assistance to states remains essential in particular when it comes to capacity building, technical training, and boosting the legal capacities and information exchange, border control, etc. Fourth, the group must avoid any uniform approach that does not take account of differing national realities between countries. Chair, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia calls for a balanced discussion that would recognize the risks that could stem from an abusive use of this technology for illicit purposes, whilst at the same time underscoring that technical progress in itself is not necessarily negative. Indeed, certain tools and new technologies can help states to improve marking, tracing, and the security of stocks, and the detection and management of registers, whilst respecting domestic legislation and international obligations. By way of conclusion, Saudi Arabia wishes to commit constructively to the work of this group. We encourage the implementation of an exchange center to exchange technical know-how and to draw on the practical experience of different countries to help states to implement their national programs and the ITI, whilst respecting national sovereignty and intellectual property rights and the legal frameworks of states. Thank you very much, Chair.

On modular weapons, REFCON 4— the REFCON 4 outcome document already commits us to a shared understanding of essential structural and control components. Practical guidance should cover consistent designation of a primary marking component, the serialization of other essential modular parts with clear visual distinction, and the common marking protocol across industry. Without that third element, the mix and match of differently marked components creates exactly the loophole that ghost guns exploit. And evidence confirms that the serial numbers are consistently the primary target of obliteration efforts. On 3D-printed weapons, the key enabler is now the digital blueprint. We see two potential tracks: regulatory measures, including criminalization of weapon-specific digital files, and technical controls on the regulated metal components that hybrid printed weapons still require. The task of this expert group is to produce guidance that that states, industry, and law enforcement can apply. This could also include endorsing the systematic recording and imaging of obliteration methods on seized weapons as good practice to enable pattern analysis across seizures and national jurisdictions. Merci, Monsieur le Président. Thank you, Chair. Allow me, first of all, to congratulate you on your election to chair this group, to chair this group, and for organizing this first meeting. France would also like to thank the panelists for their presentations. Today I'd like to share some national practices from France to address the challenges posed by developments in the manufacture, technology, and the creation of small arms and light weapons, particularly polymer weapons, modular weapons, and also illegal 3D printing. On polymer weapons, the decree from the 20th of April 2020 on marking firearms, which reflects the EU Directive 2019/68, stipulates for frames or receiver housings made by a non-metallic material— from a non-metallic material— the marking should be on a metallic plate which is durably included in the material of the housings or frames so that the plate cannot be easily taken off. But nor should it destroy part of the frames or receiver housings. The minimum depth of the marking should be 0.0762mm or 0.003 inches, and this is applicable to all types of marking, including those that are done in polymer on a metallic plaque. The metallic plaque should be strongly— solidly integrated into the polymer and visible in a window, which would be a hole in the polymer, so which means that the plaque with the marking on it is clearly visible. Other marking techniques for receiver housings and frames can be used as the manufacturer's choice, as long as these techniques have been demonstrated to show an equivalent level— to show that the marking is long-lasting and clear, and it also respects the minimum depth standards.
